questionText: Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (in force from July 1, 2024), which section defines cheating by personation, such as pretending to be a bank official or police officer over digital media?
options: Section 319 of BNS, 2023
Section 420 of IPC, 1860
Section 302 of BNS, 2023
Section 500 of BNS, 2023
explanation: Section 319 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 specifically defines cheating by personation (pretending to be someone else, or knowingly substituting one person for another). This replaces Section 416 of the erstwhile IPC.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 319 defines cheating by personation.
Incorrect. Section 420 was part of the IPC, which was repealed on July 1, 2024.
Incorrect. Section 302 of BNS deals with snatching.
Incorrect. Section 500 does not define cheating.
whyIncorrect: Offences committed on or after July 1, 2024 are governed by BNS Section 319, not the repealed IPC.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: In cyber FIRs registered after July 1, 2024, online impersonation is charged under BNS Section 319 alongside IT Act Section 66D.

questionText: A scammer creates a fake e-commerce portal and convinces buyers to transfer Rs. 45,000 for mobile phones that are never delivered. Under BNS 2023, which provision punishes cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property?
options: Section 318(4) of BNS, 2023
Section 66A of IT Act
Section 124A of IPC
Section 103 of BNS, 2023
explanation: Section 318(4) of BNS, 2023 prescribes punishment of imprisonment up to 7 years and fine for anyone who cheats and dishonestly induces delivery of property, succeeding IPC Section 420.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 318(4) directly penalizes financial cheating with up to 7 years imprisonment.
Incorrect. Section 66A of the IT Act was declared unconstitutional in 2015.
Incorrect. IPC is repealed and Section 124A was the sedition clause.
Incorrect. Section 103 relates to murder.
whyIncorrect: Relying on struck-down or repealed clauses weakens formal legal complaints; BNS Section 318(4) is the operative criminal section.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: When money is fraudulently taken in an online scam, Section 318(4) of BNS applies alongside IT Act Section 66D.

questionText: Which of the following acts constitute the offence of voyeurism under Section 77 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023? (Select all that apply)
options: Capturing the image of a woman engaging in a private act where privacy is reasonably expected
Disseminating or publishing intimate images captured in private circumstances without consent
Forwarding a publicly broadcast television news segment
Installing a covert camera in a commercial changing room
explanation: Section 77 of BNS, 2023 punishes anyone who watches, captures, or disseminates images of a woman engaging in a private act where she would reasonably expect privacy.
optionExplanations: Correct. Capturing images in private acts is voyeurism under Section 77.
Correct. Disseminating intimate images without consent is explicitly punishable under Section 77.
Incorrect. Publicly broadcast news carries no private expectation of privacy.

whyIncorrect: Only acts in private circumstances where privacy is reasonably expected fall under Section 77.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Section 77 of BNS criminalizes both capturing private acts and forwarding/disseminating non-consensual intimate imagery.

questionText: Arrange the procedural steps taken under the BNSS (Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023) when investigating a serious cyber fraud case:
sequenceItems: 1. Receipt of complaint and registration of Zero FIR or regular FIR under BNS Sections 318/319
2. Sending formal notice under Section 94 BNSS to banks and intermediaries for data preservation
3. Freezing suspicious beneficiary mule accounts under Section 106 BNSS
4. Forensic imaging and hash calculation of seized digital storage devices
5. Filing of final police report (chargesheet) before the Judicial Magistrate

whyIncorrect: Seizure and account freezing must follow formal legal notices and statutory authorization under BNSS.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Police can register a "Zero FIR" at any cyber police station irrespective of jurisdictional boundaries.

Because printouts are completely banned in courts
Because only cyber police can operate printers
Because screenshots are never allowed as evidence
explanation: Under Section 63(4) of BSA, 2023 (affirming Arjun Panditrao), electronic records produced as secondary evidence require a mandatory certificate detailing device operation and signed by a lawful manager or expert.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 63(4) requires a signed certificate affirming device integrity and accuracy.
Incorrect. Printouts are admissible when accompanied by a Section 63 certificate.
Incorrect. Any lawful device manager or expert can certify.
Incorrect. Screenshots are admissible when properly certified.
whyIncorrect: Without a Section 63 certificate proving lawful device custody, computer printouts can be excluded as inadmissible hearsay.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Always execute a Section 63 BSA certificate detailing device condition and truthfulness when presenting printed digital records.

questionText: Match each digital evidence concept with its correct legal and forensic definition under the BSA framework:

matchingPairs.right: Cryptographic fingerprint proving zero data alteration
Chronological log tracking who accessed the evidence
Exact bit-for-bit duplicate including deleted clusters
Mandatory statutory affirmation of computer integrity

explanation: Hashing proves integrity; chain of custody proves continuity; bit-stream imaging clones media; Section 63 certificate provides legal admissibility.

questionText: Order the digital evidence handling steps in correct order of volatility (from most volatile to least volatile):
sequenceItems: 2. Routing tables, ARP cache, and process memory (RAM)
3. Temporary file system storage and swap files
4. Hard disk drive storage and non-volatile NAND flash memory
5. Remote logging records and physical media backups
explanation: Order of Volatility (RFC 3227): CPU registers -> RAM & ARP cache -> Temporary swap -> Hard disk -> Remote backups.
whyIncorrect: Shutting down a computer abruptly destroys volatile RAM memory containing encryption keys and running malware processes.

questionText: Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which of the following qualify as Primary Evidence (Section 57/62)? (Select all that apply)
options: The original physical smartphone containing the authentic WhatsApp database in its internal memory
The original video camera memory card on which the security footage was recorded
A photocopied printout of a screenshot taken from a friend's laptop
A server hard drive containing the authoritative transaction database
explanation: Under BSA, the original storage medium (phone internal storage, original SD card, server drive) is Primary Evidence. Printouts, exports, and screen captures are Secondary Evidence requiring Section 63 certification.
optionExplanations: Correct. The original mobile phone is primary evidence.
Correct. The original camera memory card is primary evidence.
Incorrect. A photocopied printout is secondary evidence requiring certification.
Correct. The original server hard drive is primary evidence.
whyIncorrect: Secondary printouts require Section 63 compliance, whereas producing the original physical media constitutes primary evidence.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: If you present the original phone itself in court, it is primary evidence. If you bring a printout, it is secondary evidence requiring a Section 63 certificate.

questionText: Does Section 61 of BSA recognize electronic records as having equal legal standing to paper documents? (Evidence Rule 006)
options: Yes, under Section 61/63 of BSA, electronic records have equal legal force subject to certification standards
No, electronic records have zero legal standing in India
Only records written in handwritten ink are legal
Only records verified by international police are admissible

optionExplanations: Correct. Electronic records have full legal parity when authenticated per Section 63.
Incorrect. Electronic records are fully admissible under BSA.
Incorrect. Digital records do not require handwritten ink.
Incorrect. Domestic certification under Section 63 is the governing statutory mechanism.
whyIncorrect: Failing to recognize digital parity overlooks the core modernization objective of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

questionText: What is the operational commencement status of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP Act), 2023?
options: It was enacted in August 2023, with Section 1(2) specifying that provisions will come into force on dates appointed by Central Government notification in the Official Gazette
It came into full force on January 1, 2021
It was struck down by the Supreme Court
It is an advisory document with zero statutory status
explanation: The DPDP Act, 2023 was enacted on August 11, 2023. Under Section 1(2), its operational commencement is staggered and subject to notifications in the Official Gazette as rules and the Data Protection Board are established.
optionExplanations: Correct. DPDP Act is enacted statute with operational commencement pending Official Gazette notification.
Incorrect. It was enacted in 2023, not 2021.
Incorrect. It has not been struck down.
Incorrect. It is a full Parliamentary Act, not an advisory.
whyIncorrect: Failing to distinguish enactment from operational commencement is a critical legal accuracy error.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: DPDP Act 2023 is enacted Parliamentary law; its substantive enforcement clauses become operational via Gazette notifications.

questionText: Under Section 4 of the DPDP Act, 2023, on which grounds may a Data Fiduciary process personal data? (Select all that apply)
options: Upon obtaining the explicit consent of the Data Principal (Section 6)
For certain legitimate uses specified in Section 7 (such as employment or medical emergency)
For arbitrary commercial profit without informing the user
To fulfill statutory obligations or court orders
explanation: Under Section 4, personal data may only be processed for a lawful purpose for which the Data Principal has given consent (Section 6), or for specified legitimate uses (Section 7, e.g., emergency, state benefits, employment, legal compliance).
optionExplanations: Correct. Consent under Section 6 is the primary ground for processing.
Correct. Legitimate uses under Section 7 provide non-consent exceptions.
Incorrect. Processing without consent or legitimate statutory grounds is unlawful.
Correct. Complying with law or court decree is a recognized legitimate use.
whyIncorrect: Data fiduciaries cannot process personal data without valid consent or explicit legitimate statutory uses.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Companies cannot quietly monetize your personal data. They need either your clear consent or a recognized statutory reason.

questionText: Under Section 14 of the DPDP Act, 2023, what right is granted to a Data Principal regarding their digital assets and personal data in the event of death or incapacity?
options: Right to nominate an individual who will exercise data rights in the event of death or incapacity
All personal accounts are permanently surrendered to the state
Family members must pay a 20% estate tax to access accounts
Internet service providers automatically inherit all files
explanation: Section 14 of the DPDP Act empowers a Data Principal to nominate any other individual who shall, in the event of death or incapacity of the Data Principal, exercise the rights of the Data Principal.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 14 explicitly provides the Right to Nominate a digital heir or representative.
Incorrect. Accounts are not automatically surrendered to the state.
Incorrect. No estate tax applies to data rights.
Incorrect. ISPs do not inherit private digital assets.
whyIncorrect: Section 14 provides an innovative statutory solution for digital succession and estate planning.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: You have the right under DPDP Act Section 14 to designate a trusted person to manage your online accounts if you pass away.

A mandatory non-refundable cash deposit
A waiver of all constitutional rights

questionText: Arrange the immediate steps to take upon falling victim to an unauthorized debit transaction:
sequenceItems: 1. Block debit/credit card or disable UPI payments in your official banking app
2. Dial National Cybercrime Helpline 1930 with transaction UTR and debit account number
3. Log on to cybercrime.gov.in and register a detailed formal complaint docket
4. Submit a written dispute acknowledgment copy to your bank branch within 3 days
explanation: First stop further losses by blocking card/UPI; call 1930 within the Golden Hour; register complaint docket; submit written claim to bank.
whyIncorrect: Filing paper complaints before blocking cards allows fraudsters to continue draining funds.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Block card immediately -> Call 1930 -> File on cybercrime.gov.in -> Notify bank in writing.

questionText: True or False: Calling 1930 guarantees that 100% of your stolen money will be refunded within 24 hours without any police or magistrate paperwork.
options: True
False
explanation: False. 1930 initiates inter-bank hold requests through CFCFRMS. If the fraudster has already withdrawn the cash, freezes cannot occur. Furthermore, released funds require magistrate orders under Section 503 of BNSS.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. No system can guarantee 100% recovery if funds were already withdrawn.
Correct. 1930 coordinates holds, but recovery depends on remaining funds and judicial release orders.
whyIncorrect: Assuming recovery is guaranteed can lead to delayed prevention habits.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: 1930 maximizes freezing chances, but cannot guarantee recovery. Prevention is always your best defense.

category: Indian Cyber Law and IT Act
questionText: A police officer attempts to book a citizen under Section 66A of the IT Act for sending an offensive comment on Facebook. What is the legal status of Section 66A in Indian law?
options: Section 66A was struck down in its entirety as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal (2015), and no citizen can be legally booked under it
Section 66A is fully valid and active law
Section 66A only applies to government employees
Section 66A was amended in 2024 to double the prison term
explanation: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court held Section 66A void and unconstitutional for violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a). The Supreme Court reaffirmed in PUCL (2022) that no FIR under 66A is lawful.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 66A is void and unconstitutional.
Incorrect. Section 66A has zero legal force.
Incorrect. It was struck down for all persons.
Incorrect. It was not amended; it is omitted/void.
whyIncorrect: Invoking Section 66A reflects zombie policing; the section has been unconstitutional since 2015.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Section 66A was struck down in 2015. No citizen can be legally arrested or booked under Section 66A for social media posts.

category: Indian Cyber Law and IT Act
questionText: Which of the following sections of the IT Act, 2000 are criminal offences tried before a criminal magistrate? (Select all that apply)
options: Section 66 (Computer related offences with dishonest intent)
Section 66C (Identity theft and password misuse)
Section 66D (Cheating by personation using computer resource)
Section 43 (Civil damages and compensation for computer interference)
explanation: Sections 66, 66C, and 66D are criminal offenses carrying imprisonment and fines under Chapter XI. Section 43 is a civil liability provision under Chapter IX for compensation.
optionExplanations: Correct. Section 66 carries up to 3 years imprisonment.
Correct. Section 66C carries up to 3 years imprisonment.
Correct. Section 66D carries up to 3 years imprisonment.
Incorrect. Section 43 provides civil compensation, not criminal imprisonment.
whyIncorrect: Failing to distinguish civil compensation (Section 43) from criminal prosecution (Section 66) confuses jurisdictional filings.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Section 43 provides civil compensation before the IT Adjudicating Officer; Sections 66, 66C, and 66D are criminal offences tried by magistrates.

category: Indian Cyber Law and IT Act
questionText: True or False: Following the 2008 IT Act Amendment, Section 43 removed the original Rs. 1 crore cap, allowing Adjudicating Officers to award compensation based on actual verified injury.
options: True
False
explanation: True. The 2008 Amendment removed the phrase "not exceeding one crore rupees" from Section 43, replacing it with "damages by way of compensation", eliminating the static ceiling.
optionExplanations: Correct. The Rs. 1 crore cap was deleted by the 2008 Amendment.
Incorrect. It is true; there is no longer a fixed statutory ceiling in Section 43.
whyIncorrect: Relying on outdated 2000 textbook editions ignores the 2008 legislative amendment.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: Section 43 of the IT Act allows compensation based on actual proven loss without a fixed Rs. 1 crore cap.

category: Indian Cyber Law and IT Act
questionText: Match each IT Act section with its statutory offense and maximum imprisonment term:

matchingPairs.right: Identity theft / password theft (up to 3 years)
Cheating by personation using computer (up to 3 years)
Violation of privacy / voyeurism (up to 3 years)
Child sexual abuse material online (up to 5 years on 1st conviction)

explanation: Section 66C, 66D, and 66E carry up to 3 years; Section 67B carries up to 5 years on first conviction and 7 years on subsequent conviction.
whyIncorrect: Mixing up penalties compromises formal legal pleadings.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: IT Act sections 66C and 66D are standard charges in modern digital identity and fraud complaints.

category: Indian Cyber Law and IT Act
questionText: Under Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, who is authorized to issue directions for blocking public access to an online information resource through an authorized officer?
options: The Central Government (or designated officer not below Joint Secretary rank)
Any private bank manager
A local municipal corporator
Any private security company
explanation: Section 69A authorizes only the Central Government, on specified statutory grounds (sovereignty, defense, friendly relations, public order), to direct intermediaries to block access to online content.
optionExplanations: Correct. Only the Central Government has statutory authority under Section 69A.
Incorrect. Private bank managers have zero blocking authority.
Incorrect. Municipal corporators have no statutory authority.
Incorrect. Private companies cannot order national website blocks.
whyIncorrect: Website blocking under Section 69A is a sovereign Central Government power subject to procedural safeguards upheld in Shreya Singhal.
practicalTakeaway: Remember: National website blocking in India is governed exclusively by Section 69A of the IT Act through the Central Government.
